questions.stem: Under what assignment is the implication $p \to q$ **false**?
questions.explanation: An implication claims only that a true antecedent guarantees a true consequent, so the single way to refute it is to exhibit a true antecedent with a false consequent. When $p$ is false the implication is *vacuously* true — the promise was never triggered — which is why "if $n < 0$ then the array is sorted" is true for every non-negative $n$.

distractorRationale.b: Vacuously true: a false antecedent imposes no obligation
distractorRationale.c: Also vacuously true for the same reason
distractorRationale.d: The promise was made and kept, so the implication holds

questions.stem: How many rows does the truth table of a formula containing 4 distinct propositional variables have? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Each variable takes one of two values independently, so there are $2^n$ assignments and hence $2^4 = 16$ rows. This exponential growth is why exhaustive truth-table checking is impractical beyond about 20 variables, and it is the origin of the boolean satisfiability problem's difficulty — SAT was the first problem proved NP-complete.

questions.stem: A guard reads `if (authenticated && tokenValid)`. Which condition is logically equivalent to its negation?
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law states $\lnot(p \wedge q) \equiv \lnot p \vee \lnot q$: the conjunction fails as soon as *either* conjunct fails, so the negation is a disjunction. Distributing the negation while leaving `&&` in place is the single most common error in writing an `else` branch, and it produces a guard that is strictly too narrow.

distractorRationale.a: Negates each operand but keeps the conjunction; this is $\lnot(p \vee q)$, true only when both fail
distractorRationale.c: Equivalent to option a by the other De Morgan law, so it has the same defect
distractorRationale.d: Drops the negations entirely, giving a formula that is true in three of the four rows

questions.stem: What is the **contrapositive** of "If the cache is warm, then the query is fast"?

options.text: If the query is fast, then the cache is warm
If the cache is not warm, then the query is not fast
If the query is not fast, then the cache is not warm
The cache is warm and the query is not fast

questions.explanation: The contrapositive of $p \to q$ is $\lnot q \to \lnot p$ — negate both parts *and* swap them. It is logically equivalent to the original, which makes it a legitimate proof strategy: proving that a slow query implies a cold cache establishes the original claim exactly.

distractorRationale.a: That is the converse $q \to p$, which is not equivalent — the query might be fast for another reason
distractorRationale.b: That is the inverse $\lnot p \to \lnot q$, also not equivalent; it is the converse of the contrapositive
distractorRationale.d: That is the negation $p \wedge \lnot q$, which contradicts the original rather than restating it

questions.stem: Given $p$ = true, $q$ = false and $r$ = true, evaluate $(p \wedge \lnot q) \to (q \wedge r)$.

options.text: Undefined, because $q$ appears on both sides
True only if the implication is read as a biconditional

questions.explanation: Evaluate innermost first. The antecedent $p \wedge \lnot q$ is $\text{T} \wedge \text{T} = \text{T}$. The consequent $q \wedge r$ is $\text{F} \wedge \text{T} = \text{F}$. A true antecedent with a false consequent is the one assignment that makes an implication false, so the formula evaluates to false.

distractorRationale.a: Would follow from treating the implication as vacuously true, but the antecedent here is genuinely true
distractorRationale.c: A variable may occur any number of times; each occurrence simply takes its assigned value
distractorRationale.d: A biconditional would also be false here, since the two sides differ

questions.stem: Which formula is logically equivalent to $p \to q$?
questions.explanation: Both formulae are false on exactly one assignment, $p$ true and $q$ false, and true on the other three, so their truth tables agree. This identity is why implication is not a primitive connective in most normal forms: any formula can be rewritten using only $\lnot$, $\wedge$ and $\vee$, which is the first step in converting to conjunctive normal form for a SAT solver.

distractorRationale.b: This is $q \to p$, the converse, false when $q$ is true and $p$ false
distractorRationale.c: True on only one assignment out of four, so it cannot match an implication
distractorRationale.d: This is the *negation* of $p \to q$, true exactly where the implication is false

questions.stem: "If the build is broken, the tests fail. The tests failed. Therefore the build is broken." What is wrong with this argument?

options.text: It affirms the consequent: from $p \to q$ and $q$ one cannot conclude $p$, because $q$ may have other causes
It denies the antecedent, which is invalid
It is invalid because the premises are empirically false

questions.explanation: The premises are $p \to q$ and $q$, and the conclusion $p$ does not follow — the implication permits $q$ to be true while $p$ is false, which is precisely the case of a flaky test failing on a perfectly good build. Modus ponens requires the *antecedent* as the second premise; taking the consequent instead is the fallacy of affirming the consequent, and the valid inference from $q$'s negation would be modus tollens.

distractorRationale.a: Modus ponens is $p \to q$ together with $p$, concluding $q$; here the second premise is $q$
distractorRationale.c: Denying the antecedent is a different fallacy, arguing from $\lnot p$ to $\lnot q$
distractorRationale.d: Validity concerns the *form* of an argument; an argument can be valid with false premises and invalid with true ones

options.text: From $p \to q$ and $\lnot p$, conclude $\lnot q$
From $p \to q$ and $\lnot q$, conclude $\lnot p$

questions.explanation: That is **modus tollens**. If $p$ were true then $q$ would follow from the implication, contradicting $\lnot q$; so $p$ must be false. Equivalently it is modus ponens applied to the contrapositive $\lnot q \to \lnot p$. In practice this is how a failing assertion is used to rule out a hypothesis about a bug.

distractorRationale.a: Denying the antecedent — $q$ may hold for reasons unrelated to $p$
distractorRationale.c: Affirming the consequent — the implication does not forbid $q$ without $p$
distractorRationale.d: Inclusive $\vee$ permits both disjuncts to be true, so $p$ tells us nothing about $q$; the inference would need exclusive or

questions.stem: The formula $(p \to q) \vee (q \to p)$ is a tautology.
questions.explanation: True, and the reason is instructive. An implication can only fail when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. For both disjuncts to fail at once we would need $p$ true with $q$ false *and* $q$ true with $p$ false — a contradiction. So at least one disjunct holds on every one of the four assignments, and the disjunction is a tautology. Checking the table directly confirms it: T, T, T, T.
